headline: Peanut Bunker Pile Up at the Shoal — Blues Follow the Squeeze
subhead: Bait funneling through the Stratford Shoal narrows is dragging bluefish east and holding stripers deep until the new moon flips the tide.
body_markdown:
I spent Tuesday morning just watching before I made a cast. That's the job half the time out here — you don't fish the fleet, you fish the bait, and right now the bait is telling a clear story around the Shoal. Peanut bunker are pouring through the Stratford Shoal narrows in tight, nervous pods, pushed by current and squeezed by the way the Sound pinches down through the middle. Mixed in with them are bay anchovies flickering silver on the surface at first light off Charles Island, and I'm seeing silversides stacked thick along the Norwalk Islands flats on the last of the outgoing. When bait gets funneled like this — physically compressed by the geography instead of just schooled up on its own — it draws attention fast. That's exactly what's happening.

Kings Point is reading warm, 70.9°F, and New London on the eastern end is a touch cooler at 69.4. That gradient matters. It means the Central Sound right now — Stratford Shoal on down through the Norwalks — is holding the warmest, most stable water in the zone, and it's acting like a lid that keeps bait and gamefish concentrated rather than spread thin. Bluefish have been rebuilding out of the deeper reef structure to our west — Middle Ground, 11B, 28C — and that push is exactly what I've been watching move east through the week. I had a solid run of blues to 6 and 7 pounds working bunker pods over the Middle Ground Light rip on the last two hours of the outgoing, casting Hopkins jigs and metal-lip poppers into the surface wash where the bait was getting pinned against the current. If you see birds working tight and low instead of high and scattered, that's usually blues underneath, not just gulls picking scraps.

Striped bass are still playing the deep and dark game we called out last week — said the deep/night pattern would hold until the new moon tides started stirring things up, and that's still exactly where we are. Daytime bites have been sluggish and short-lived, mostly at first light and last light, with the better fish coming off the bottom in 30 to 45 feet along the Stratford Shoal rip and the drop-offs east of the Norwalk Islands. Plastic eels — 9-inch black or dark purple — fished slow on a 3-way rig with 2 to 3 ounces of lead, dragged right along bottom on the last of the ebb, have been the most consistent producer. A few boats working bucktails tipped with a strip of squid have connected after dark drifting the Charles Island flats, picking up fish in the mid-20s to low-30s, nothing gigantic but steady enough to make the trip worthwhile if you're willing to fish the clock instead of the calendar.

Porgies remain the one bite you can set a watch by. Structure around the Norwalk Islands and the rockier stretches off Charles Island are stacked with them — bloodworms and clam strips on a simple two-hook bottom rig in 15 to 25 feet, best on the last two hours of the incoming when the current slacks enough to hold bottom without a half-pound of lead. Nothing flashy, but it's the bite that never lets you down out here in August.

Fluke have been the frustrating one. Small fish dominating the counts in the western half of my zone — lots of 14 to 16 inchers around Oyster Bay and the Huntington-side flats — with only occasional keepers mixed in. I haven't heard of anyone tearing it up on the drift with bucktails and Gulp this week; it's more a game of covering ground and culling through shorts than locking onto a pattern. If you're set on fluke, I'd fish the sandier bottom east of Port Jefferson Harbor on the outgoing, working white and chartreuse 4-inch Gulp swimming mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, slow and tight to bottom.

Weakfish have shown up only as incidental catches — a couple mentioned taken at dusk on soft plastics fished for bass — nothing you could call a pattern yet, more a reminder they're still out there than a reason to target them specifically.

Looking ahead, the tidal range is building hard into the August 12 new moon, and that's the piece I'm watching closest. Bigger swings mean stronger current at every rip and edge in this zone — the Shoal, the Norwalk reefs, the Middle Ground — and stronger current usually means the deep/night bass pattern finally cracks open into something more aggressive on the moving tides. If the bluefish push continues sliding east the way it has all week, I'd expect blues showing more consistently around the Norwalk Islands and even pushing toward the Connecticut shoreline by the weekend. And with bonito already working their way west out of Rhode Island waters, it's worth keeping half an eye on the eastern end of my beat — Charles Island and beyond — for the first sign of them showing up as the current sharpens and the bait keeps getting squeezed through this narrow stretch of Sound. I wouldn't plan a whole trip around it yet, but I'd have a small metal or an epoxy jig rigged just in case.
